name: Matilda Betham-Edwards
credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Matilda Betham-Edwards (1836–1919) was an English novelist, travel writer and Francophile, and a prolific poet, who also wrote a number of children's books.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poems.title: A Valentine
poems.author: Matilda Betham-Edwards
poems.collection: The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (1912)
poems.text:
What shall I send my love to-day,
When all the woods attune to love,
And I would show the lark and dove
That I can love as well as they?...

I'll send a kiss, for that would be
The quickest sent, the lightest borne;
And well I know to-morrow morn
She'll send it back again to me.

Go, happy winds! ah, do not stay
Enamour'd of my lady's cheek,
But hasten home, and I'll bespeak
Your services another day!

poems.title: The Pansy and the Prayer-Book
poems.author: Matilda Betham-Edwards
poems.collection: The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (1912)
poems.text:
Following across the moors a sound of bells,
We found a church, the smallest that could be,
Hid in a tamarisk-grove beside the sea,
And graves of shipwreck'd men set round with shells.
We enter'd when the prayers were almost done:
The little children nodded on their knees,
The preacher's voice was drown'd in hum of bees
That danced about the lectern in the sun.

Awhile we knelt I let a pansy glide
Between her sweet grave face and open book,
And whisper'd as she turn'd with chiding look —
'Heaven has not will'd, dear heart, that aught divide
Love pure as ours, nor blames if thought of me
Come like this flower between thy God and thee,'
